summary: Computer-vision safety monitoring, BIM clash detection, and autonomous site scanning are the working deployments - the sector's AI mostly watches the jobsite and checks the model against reality before concrete is poured.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Business Outlook Survey measured AI use among construction firms at 14.3 percent in its latest reading, down slightly from 14.9 percent in the prior period. These figures come from firms answering, fortnightly, whether they used AI in the preceding two weeks, making construction one of the more consistently tracked sectors in the series. The modest dip between periods is worth noting but should not be overstated given the survey's short reference window and the natural variability of fortnightly snapshots.

Within the industry, the applications drawing the most attention cluster around computer-vision safety monitoring, building information modeling clash detection, and autonomous site scanning. BuiltWorlds, the construction-technology research network that tracks site robotics, jobsite IoT, and digital preconstruction across its member benchmarking programs, has organized dedicated conference programming around AI and machine learning specifically for the architecture, engineering, construction, and owner sector. Its annual AI/ML Conference covers existing and emerging use cases across the full construction and building operation process, including implementation strategies at both the project and enterprise levels and case studies on lessons learned.

The Associated General Contractors of America, which represents over 27,000 member firms, surveys technology adoption and safety-technology compliance across U.S. builders and has positioned its own events around practical AI implementation, convening construction leaders, technology experts, and AI practitioners across dedicated tracks. AGC's data functions as the primary adoption record for the contractor community, and the organization's engagement with AI topics signals that the subject has moved from experimental to a recognized area of professional development for project executives.

On the capital side, CREtech and MetaProp track venture flow across architecture, engineering, and construction technology alongside property technology more broadly. The sources do not provide specific investment figures, but the inclusion of AEC within proptech venture tracking reflects an acknowledged overlap between real-estate technology and construction technology as investors allocate to the built-environment stack.

For a firm deciding whether to deploy AI, the Census data suggest that roughly one in seven construction companies is already doing so in any given two-week window, which means early-mover advantage is narrowing but the majority of the industry has not yet committed. BuiltWorlds and AGC both offer benchmarking and peer case studies that would help a firm assess where its own readiness sits relative to the contractor community. The sources reviewed here do not report specific ROI figures, regulatory constraints, or quantified risk findings for construction AI, so a deployment decision should be supplemented with more granular due diligence than this survey-level data alone can support.
